people.identity_note: Betham’s manuscript pedigree of Archibald Glasgow, Rathmalton clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, expressly names Margaret as his only daughter, married to an unnamed Cairns, with son Thomas Cairns. This proves the documentary father–daughter pair. Glasgow-3186, wife of George Lyell in South Leith in 1633, remains a candidate because a later Cairns marriage is possible, but no marriage or household bridge is proved. The Scottish Archibald profile identity remains qualified; no profile father upgrade follows. Glasgow-1523’s cited 1638 baptism names father William Glasgow, a concrete father conflict; its guessed 1642 death is not evidence. Working-model review, 16 October 2026: Select William Glasgow-3075, the Leith mealmaker, as the low-confidence working father of Margaret Glasgow-3186, indexed marrying George Lyell at South Leith on 28 November 1633. William’s household is documented at Leith, with a proposed 10 July 1610 local marriage and a son Archibald baptised in 1618, securely linked to the adult mealmaker by the 1639 apprenticeship and 1647 service of heir. A daughter marrying in 1633 fits that established household generation. Shared surname, the same parish and a coherent marriage/child generation favour this named household over a newly invented father. No source calls Margaret his daughter. Her circa-1610 birth remains an inherited estimate and supplies no independent evidence of William’s paternity. Retain the strongest specific alternative: Betham’s pedigree of Archibald Glasgow, Rathmalton clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, names Margaret as his only daughter, wife of an unnamed Cairns and mother of Thomas Cairns. The documentary father–daughter relationship is explicit, but identifying that Margaret with Glasgow-3186 remains unproved. A first Lyell marriage in 1633 permits a later Cairns marriage. The preferred William placement avoids requiring that unproved Scottish–Irish identity and remarriage. It also avoids tension with the probable identification of Archibald Glasgow-1101 as the child baptised in Glasgow in 1614 and the 1635 graduate: that child would be an implausible father of a 1633 bride. This is a ranking consideration, not an exclusion: the Scottish identity is unproved, and a baptism is not necessarily an infant’s birth. The new uncertain William field must not be used as a concrete father conflict to reject the Rathmalton candidate. A different South Leith Glasgow father also remains possible. No mother is selected: Catherine Fraith/Fraser’s 1610 bride identity and Christian Scot’s separate Glasgow household remain qualified. William’s testament names Archibald as lawful son and sole executor, not only child; omission of Margaret neither excludes her nor proves kinship. == Biography ==
Betham’s abstract of Archibald Glasgow of Rathmalton, clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, names his wife Elizabeth, Thomas Glasgow as eldest son and Margaret as only daughter. Margaret’s husband is an unnamed Cairns, and Thomas Cairns is her son.<ref>Archibald Glasgow’s will abstract names his eldest son Thomas; https://catalogue.nli.ie/Record/vtls000540633. Betham’s pre-destruction derivative abstract was inspected, not the original will. The father–son statement is explicit; identification of the son with Glasgow-3556 remains strongly probable, with no residence or estate bridge. Elizabeth’s surname remains provisional.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
Betham’s manuscript pedigree of Archibald Glasgow, Rathmalton clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, expressly names Margaret as his only daughter, married to an unnamed Cairns, with son Thomas Cairns. This proves the documentary father–daughter pair. [[Glasgow-3186]], wife of George Lyell in South Leith in 1633, remains a candidate because a later Cairns marriage is possible, but no marriage or household bridge is proved. The Scottish Archibald profile identity remains qualified; no profile father upgrade follows. [[Glasgow-1523]]’s cited 1638 baptism names father William Glasgow, a concrete father conflict; its guessed 1642 death is not evidence. Working-model review, 16 October 2026: Select William [[Glasgow-3075]], the Leith mealmaker, as the low-confidence working father of Margaret [[Glasgow-3186]], indexed marrying George Lyell at South Leith on 28 November 1633. William’s household is documented at Leith, with a proposed 10 July 1610 local marriage and a son Archibald baptised in 1618, securely linked to the adult mealmaker by the 1639 apprenticeship and 1647 service of heir. A daughter marrying in 1633 fits that established household generation. Shared surname, the same parish and a coherent marriage/child generation favour this named household over a newly invented father. No source calls Margaret his daughter. Her [[circa-1610]] birth remains an inherited estimate and supplies no independent evidence of William’s paternity. Retain the strongest specific alternative: Betham’s pedigree of Archibald Glasgow, Rathmalton clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, names Margaret as his only daughter, wife of an unnamed Cairns and mother of Thomas Cairns. The documentary father–daughter relationship is explicit, but identifying that Margaret with [[Glasgow-3186]] remains unproved. A first Lyell marriage in 1633 permits a later Cairns marriage. The preferred William placement avoids requiring that unproved Scottish–Irish identity and remarriage. It also avoids tension with the probable identification of Archibald [[Glasgow-1101]] as the child baptised in Glasgow in 1614 and the 1635 graduate: that child would be an implausible father of a 1633 bride. This is a ranking consideration, not an exclusion: the Scottish identity is unproved, and a baptism is not necessarily an infant’s birth. The new uncertain William field must not be used as a concrete father conflict to reject the Rathmalton candidate. A different South Leith Glasgow father also remains possible. No mother is selected: Catherine Fraith/Fraser’s 1610 bride identity and Christian Scot’s separate Glasgow household remain qualified. William’s testament names Archibald as lawful son and sole executor, not only child; omission of Margaret neither excludes her nor proves kinship. [[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
Daniel Glasco/Glascow, Norfolk planter, conveys 100 acres to Richard Linton with the consent of Mary, explicitly his wife, from Henry Slade’s 330-acre patent. The deed was recorded on 3 September 1729; the upper endorsement expressly says Daniel came into court and acknowledged it, proving him alive on that date.<ref>Princess Anne County, Deeds and Wills Book4 Part1 (1724–1735), manuscript p.207, DGS7645780; https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-99PX-F3DX. Original deed-book image partly read at limited resolution. Exact execution dates and the earlier William title recital remain provisional. No father clause was inspected; Daniel’s identity remains unresolved. William Glasgow-428 is not named; the linked profile preserves the associated property-trail research.</ref>

Daneill Glasco witnesses Richard Johnson’s Norfolk will dated 26 February 1729/30, with Richard Linton and John Moy. The will was proved on 18 September 1730.<ref>Unidentified Daneill Glasco witnesses a Norfolk will; https://www.familysearch.org/library/books/viewer/166084/. McIntosh, printed p.122 (not112), visually inspected; not the original will manuscript. The witness’s identity with either Daniel profile is unresolved. No father or survival-to-probate inference. William Glasgow-428 is an associated research case and is not named in this entry.</ref>

The upper endorsement expressly says Daniel came into court and acknowledged the act on 3 September 1729, proving him alive then. [[Glasgow-3322]], Mary Gamon’s husband in 1693, remains compatible, but the two estates have no proved continuous title chain. Original deed-book image partly read at limited resolution. Exact execution dates and the earlier William title recital remain provisional. No father clause was inspected; Daniel’s identity remains unresolved. William Glasgow-428 is not named; the linked profile preserves the associated property-trail research.</ref>

The 1912 Belfast and Ulster Directory lists Robert McCaughern, farmer, Lisnagaver in the neighbourhood section for Rasharkin. It is a useful later locality lead because Lisnagaver is the Glasgow family's documented townland and the directory places a McCaughern farmer there after the 1851 and 1901–1911 census evidence.<ref>1912 Belfast and Ulster Directory, Rasharkin; https://lennonwylie.co.uk/PT191214.htm; . The original 1911 Lisnagaver return identifies Robert McCaughern, 54, farmer, with wife Mary Anne, 58; married 28 years, both Antrim-born Church of Ireland. The occupation and exact locality strongly identify the 1912 directory farmer. His parents are not stated.<ref>1911 Lisnagaver, Robert McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001389352.pdf; Form A; official index house 2; printed number altered; rows 1–2. [[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

The published headstone transcription for Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church records a memorial erected by Alexander Elder of Gortrickey to his father Robert Elder, his mother Jane, and his sisters and brothers. It also records Alexander Elder's death on 5 January 1943.<ref>Rasharkin Second Presbyterian Church headstones; https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/graveyard.html; . This is a new direct memorial transcription for the catalogue's parentage study, not a Glasgow record and not proof that the Elder family was related to Alexander Glasgow. Its value is locality context: Gortrickey/Gortereghy is the townland where the Glasgow family appears in the 1837–1838 Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism entries. The memorial supplies a named Elder household for future comparison with the later Robert Elder who occupied Alexander Glasgow's former Lisnagaver lot; identity between those Elder references remains unproved.</ref>

A 2007 RootsChat research post reproduces a 18 June 1908 Second Portglenone Presbyterian marriage entry for Alexander Elder, full-age bachelor farmer of Gortreaghy, whose father is recorded as Robert Elder, farmer. Alexander married Mary Anderson, full-age spinster of Gortreaghy, daughter of Neil Anderson; witnesses were Robert Anderson and Margaret Elder.<ref>RootsChat, Elder, Murdoch & McMeekin Families; https://www.rootschat.com/forum/index.php?topic=214109.0; . The entry is not yet an inspected original, so it is a secondary-source lead rather than final evidence. It is nevertheless a new, specific parent-bearing record for the Gortreaghy Elder household and gives a testable route for determining whether the Alexander Elder on the Rasharkin Second Presbyterian memorial was a son of the Robert Elder who later occupied Alexander Glasgow's Lisnagaver lot. That identity chain remains unproved.</ref>

The inspected original 1911 Gortereghy census return records Alexander Elder, aged 40, as head, Mary Elder, aged 44, as wife, Robert Elder, aged 34, as brother, and Margaret Elder, aged 25, as sister (Form A, official index house 37, nai001390156, rows 1–4). These stated relationships support comparison with the 1901 household, the 1908 marriage lead and the Rasharkin Second Presbyterian memorial; identification with existing profiles remains qualified.<ref>1911 Gortereghy, Alexander Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390156.pdf; Form A; official index house 37; rows 1–4. Original register or Form A inspected on 30 September 2026; source-specific image and entry references supplied. Profile identities and cross-record continuity remain qualified where stated.</ref>

The original 1901 Gortereghy return records Robert Elder, 65, widowed farmer, with Alex 27 and Robert 20 as sons and Eliza 22 and Margaretta 14 as daughters. The 1911 Alexander/Mary household explicitly records Robert as Alexander’s brother and Margaret as his sister. The combined names and locality strongly support continuity, with age differences retained. Robert [[Elder-7144]] remains a qualified father identity; Robert/Mary Glasgow’s Gortahar household is separate.<ref>1901 Gortereghy, Robert Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai000298460.pdf; Form A; official index house 42; rows 1–5; 1911 Gortereghy, Alexander Elder household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390156.pdf; Form A; official index house 37; rows 1–4. Inspected original record; profile identity remains qualified where stated.</ref>

Together with the 1908 Alexander/Mary Anderson marriage extract, these support one sibling family. Retain the actual age differences. No matching Alexander profile was established in full same-name and father-filtered searches.

A reproduced Second Portglenone Presbyterian marriage list records John Elder, full-age bachelor of Rasharkin, marrying Annie Patterson, aged 20, on 12 May 1886. John's father is recorded as John Elder, farmer; Annie's father as David Patterson, farmer.<ref>Second Portglenone Presbyterian civil marriage 1886; https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1886/10833/5951328.pdf; printed page 53; PDF page 1; entry 86. The 1912 Belfast and Ulster Directory lists John Elder, junior, as a grocer and postmaster among the inhabitants of Rasharkin. == Biography ==

A fresh audit of the surviving Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription located a second parent-bearing McCaughern/Macaw household at the target townland. Hugh Macaw was born 3 February 1839 and baptised 3 March 1839 as the son of William and Mary Kilpatrick, resident at Lisnagaver (entry 125).<ref>Rasharkin Presbyterian baptisms, entries 125 and 204; https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html; . The same register records Jane Matilda Macaw, born 26 July 1843 and baptised 14 January 1844, as the daughter of William and Mary Kilpatrick at Granagh (entry 204). Named transcription reread 30 September 2026; originalmanuscriptuninspected.</ref>

Rereading Rasharkin baptism transcription entry 125 gives Hugh Macaw’s birth as 3 February 1839, replacing the maintained 5 February wording. His baptism remains 3 March 1839; original manuscript inspection is required before treating the corrected transcription as a final date.<ref>Rasharkin Presbyterian baptism transcription; https://genealogy.torrens.org/BannValley/church/RasharkinP/Baptisms_1834.html; transcription entries 125 and 204; original MIC/1P/292 uninspected. Named transcription reread; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

The freshly inspected published baptism transcription, row 125, gives birth on 3 February 1839 and baptism on 3 March, whereas the maintained handoff gave 5 February. The original image is still needed to settle the date. Consolidate Hugh and Jane Matilda with the same named parental couple. Rereading the transcription gives 3 February 1839, with the manuscript still uninspected. Parent profile identities remain uncertain; later spouses alone do not exclude an earlier family.

== Biography ==

The 1911 Gortereghy census browse records Sarah McCaughern, aged 82, as head of household with Matilda Mulholland, 52, and Caroline McCaughern, 47, recorded as daughters; Sara Jane McCaughern, 45, and Jas Alex McCaughern, 43, are also listed as children, with Geo Mulholland, 14, as grandson. It confirms a substantial McCaughern household in the same townland as the Elder and Glasgow-associated records, but it does not identify Sarah's husband, parents or relationship to Mary Glasgow.<ref>1911 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390134.pdf; Form A; official index house 26; rows 1–6. Original register or Form A inspected on 30 September 2026; source-specific image and entry references supplied. Profile identities and cross-record continuity remain qualified where stated.</ref>

The original 1901 and 1911 returns establish continuity of Sarah McCaughern’s Gortereghy family. Sarah was a Derry-born widow aged 72/82; Caroline, Sarah J/Sara Jane, James A/Jas Alex, Matilda and grandson George occur in both returns. Elizabeth, 32, is also a daughter in 1901. Sarah [[Dysart-1893]], married in 1851 to Gortereghy farmer John McCaughern, remains the strongest mother identity, but neither census names her deceased husband or maiden surname.<ref>1901 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai000298441.pdf; Form A; official index house 18; rows 1–7; 1911 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390134.pdf; Form A; official index house 26; rows 1–6; Rasharkin Presbyterian civil marriage register 1851; https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1851/09402/5405894.pdf; PDF page 1; entry 28. Inspected original record; profile identity remains qualified where stated.</ref>

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

The 1911 Gortereghy census browse records Sarah McCaughern, aged 82, as head of household with Matilda Mulholland, 52, and Caroline McCaughern, 47, recorded as daughters; Sara Jane McCaughern, 45, and Jas Alex McCaughern, 43, are also listed as children, with Geo Mulholland, 14, as grandson. It confirms a substantial McCaughern household in the same townland as the Elder and Glasgow-associated records, but it does not identify Sarah's husband, parents or relationship to Mary Glasgow.<ref>1911 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390134.pdf; Form A; official index house 26; rows 1–6. Original register or Form A inspected on 30 September 2026; source-specific image and entry references supplied. Profile identities and cross-record continuity remain qualified where stated.</ref>

The original 1901 and 1911 returns establish continuity of Sarah McCaughern’s Gortereghy family. Sarah was a Derry-born widow aged 72/82; Caroline, Sarah J/Sara Jane, James A/Jas Alex, Matilda and grandson George occur in both returns. Elizabeth, 32, is also a daughter in 1901. Sarah [[Dysart-1893]], married in 1851 to Gortereghy farmer John McCaughern, remains the strongest mother identity, but neither census names her deceased husband or maiden surname.<ref>1901 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai000298441.pdf; Form A; official index house 18; rows 1–7; 1911 Gortereghy, Sarah McCaughern household; https://api-census.nationalarchives.ie/census/image/nai001390134.pdf; Form A; official index house 26; rows 1–6; Rasharkin Presbyterian civil marriage register 1851; https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/files/civil/marriage_returns/marriages_1851/09402/5405894.pdf; PDF page 1; entry 28. Inspected original record; profile identity remains qualified where stated.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Identity revalidation, 17 October 2026: The completed George Mulholland search identified no supported Gortereghy boy born about 1897 with grandmother Sarah. The household calls Geo a grandson of Sarah, not explicitly a son of Matilda; preserve the relationship actually stated. The original 1901/1911 returns establish the household’s continuity. Dysart-1893 remains the qualified identity of grandmother Sarah. Neither this return nor the earlier return names George’s parents; Matilda as mother is a plausible comparison, not an asserted attachment.

The banns/marriage index records Anna Glasgow and THOMAS GRAY/FR49 (FR49) on 1676-06-16 at Kirknewton and East Calder.<ref>Scotland’s People: Old Parish Registers — banns and marriages: OPR 690/10 / 80; https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/. people.wikitext:
== Biography ==
David Mathy and Mergaret Androsoune, expressly his spouse, bought a barn at Powdrait, Glasgow, from John Hawstoune on 3 February 1550/51. The property adjoined Peter Adam’s land west, James Hyndschaw’s east, the street north, and Malindin or burn south.<ref>Robert Renwick, ed., ''Abstracts of Protocols of the Town Clerks of Glasgow'', vol.1, protocol71, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsofproto01glas/page/n60/mode/1up p.27]; page image inspected 30 September 2026.</ref>

A David Mathy was expressly a fellow Glasgow burgess with Robert Glesgw among witnesses to John Androsoune’s sasine on 10 May 1554. The same-day act in protocol184 had the same witnesses.<ref>Renwick, ''Abstracts of Protocols'', vol.1, protocols183–184, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsofproto01glas/page/n96/mode/1up p.63]; page image inspected 30 September 2026.</ref> David also witnessed a transaction on 4 July 1554.<ref>Renwick, ''Abstracts of Protocols'', vol.1, protocol189, [https://archive.org/details/abstractsofproto01glas/page/n98/mode/1up p.65]; page image inspected 30 September 2026.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
David Mathy and Mergaret Androsoune, expressly his spouse, bought a barn at Powdrait, Glasgow, on 3 February 1550/51. David Mathy and Robert Glesgw were expressly fellow burgesses witnessing a sasine on 10 May 1554; David also witnessed an act on 4 July 1554. The name and city make the purchaser and witness probably the same man, but the later acts do not repeat the spouse. No kinship with Robert is stated. David [[Matthew-330]] is a weak compatible variant candidate: its only 1701 death assertion is GEDCOM-derived, so it cannot be excluded. The complete sourced draft remains on HOLD against that candidate, with purchaser/witness identity qualified. Revalidated 17 October 2026 against maintained profile evidence; source readings and earlier search dates are inherited unless an explicit fresh getProfile is listed.

The purchaser and later witness are probably the same man by name and Glasgow property/civic context, but the 1554 acts do not name his wife. No inspected entry calls him kin of Robert Glesgw or names his parents. The 1550/51 transaction proves the documentary marriage, not an existing profile identity for either spouse. Margaret Anderson-3241 is a sparse compatible spouse candidate, with unknown dates and unsupported family; identity remains unresolved. The companion subject draft records her separately with the same qualification. [[Matthew-330|David Matthew]] remains a weak compatible variant candidate because its 1701 death is an unsupported GEDCOM field; do not exclude it or create another David solely from that field.

== Biography ==
'''James Glasgow''' appears in a shipping report headed ''Greenock, August 12'', published on 18 August 1740. The arrival list reads: “The Prosperity of Irvine, James Glasgow, from Northcopen.”<ref>''The Caledonian Mercury'', 18 August 1740, page 3, Greenock shipping list. [https://www.newspapers.com/image/394559372/ Newspapers.com image 394559372], original scan inspected 2 October 2026.</ref>

The list places his name in the position used for a ship's master. The report therefore supports identifying him as the master of the ''Prosperity of Irvine''. No age, relatives or personal residence is given. His birth and death remain unknown.

== Research Notes ==
Original 1740 shipping passage inspected. Four live Irvine biographies remain compatible; no occupation, age or family bridge identifies the master. No occupational or family bridge selects one of them. Other historical namesakes have not been excluded solely for missing locality fields.

== Biography ==
Nicholas Glasco is named in a 20 June 1746 report in the ''Weekly Worcester Journal'' among officers in the rebel army committed to New Gaol, Southwark. The notice lists him between John Duncan and Alexander M'Laughlan. It gives no rank for Nicholas individually and does not state a conviction, birthplace, residence, relatives, occupation, or dates of birth or death.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1214317653/ ''Weekly Worcester Journal'', 20 June 1746, p.4], original roster inspected 4 October 2026. Date follows provider metadata; masthead date has not been separately checked.</ref>


The 27 and 28 June reports describe Nicholas Glascoe as a self-styled major and allege a role in the attack on the Hazard sloop. These are allegations, not a finding of guilt.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394536822/ The Derby Mercury, 1746-06-27, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404059808/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-06-28, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

An August report lists Nicholas among persons indicted for high treason, while the 7 November paper announces the pending trial.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404060798/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-08-23, p.2], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394542827/ The Derby Mercury, 1746-11-07, p.3], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

The 8 and 17 November reports say he was acquitted, with defence evidence identifying him as a French native born at Saint-Germain-en-Laye and a lieutenant in Dillon’s Regiment. They report an order to detain him as a French prisoner. The Caledonian account also mentions a Not Guilty verdict and removal of his bolts; the saved excerpt stops before the full cartel articles. These reports require comparison with the underlying legal and military records.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404061824/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1746-11-08, p.3], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/394462695/ The Caledonian Mercury, 1746-11-17, p.2], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

In May 1747 a notice names Mr Glascoe as major in Lord Ogilvy’s new regiment. Nicholas is a probable contextual candidate, but the missing forename and unproved continuity prevent a firm identification.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/404076485/ The Newcastle Weekly Courant, 1747-05-09, p.1], original passage visually inspected 5 October 2026; issue metadata supplied by Newspapers.com.</ref>

No parents, spouse, children, birth date, death date or Irish origin is established.

Further original issues preserve June rosters, indictment reprints and Dutch reports, along with acquittal reports containing translated cartel articles. These are related issue appearances; no independent family identity follows. <ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/979338930/ The Western Flying Post; or, Sherborne and Yeovil Mercury (The Sherborne Mercury, or Weekly Advertiser), 1746-06-30, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1334222061/ S Gravenhaegse Courant, 1746-09-21, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/979339079/ The Western Flying Post; or, Sherborne and Yeovil Mercury, 1746-11-17, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971385255/ The Gloucester Journal, 1746-11-18, p.2], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1334158733/ Opregte Haarlemsche Courant, 1746-12-01, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref>

The Gloucester Journal of 28 April 1747 describes Major Glascoe as lately discharged at London and chief major in Lord Ogilvy’s projected regiment. Nicholas is a probable contextual candidate; no forename is given, and English pay is not interpreted as British military service.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971516263/ Gloucester Journal, 28 April 1747, p.1], original passage inspected 5 October 2026.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The rare full name, Southwark proceedings and Hazard episode support a probable association across the 1746 reports. French birth and service are reported defence evidence. They do not establish an Irish origin, a Glasgow-family connection or relatives. The May 1747 appointment lacks a forename.

James Glasco is reported in the marriage column published on 5 September 1786 as a publican of Omagh, aged 61, marrying Jane Murray of the same place, aged 16.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050075355/ Freeman’s Journal, 5 September 1786, p.3], original inspected 5 October 2026.</ref> If accurate, the reported ages imply approximate births in 1724–1725 and 1769–1770 respectively. Advertisements in the Northern Star on 11, 18 and 25 May 1793 name Mr. James Glasco, Omagh, as a freight or passage contact for the Hope, sailing to Newcastle and Philadelphia. The 25 May copy postpones sailing to the 25th instant.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021067/ Northern Star, 11 May 1793, p.1]; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021086/ Northern Star, 18 May 1793, p.4]; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021100/ Northern Star, 25 May 1793, p.1], originals inspected 5 October 2026.</ref> These probably concern the same Omagh man. == Biography ==
William Glasgow traded as a grocer in Belfast. A notice dated 30 October 1820 announced his move from Rosemary Street to shop and stores at 34 Smith Street, with teas, sugars and other groceries for sale.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/61259418/ The Irishman, 3 November 1820, p.1].</ref> A Belfast banks notice also lists a William Glasgow among its June 1820 signatories; the signature does not independently identify the grocer.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/61258642/ The Irishman, 16 June 1820, p.3].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/61258687/ The Irishman, 23 June 1820, p. 3, reprint of 15 June Belfast banks notice], original reprint/alternate scan checked 2026-10-05.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
3814 (c.1796–1883), a source-described retired Cookstown merchant, is an additional weak compatible candidate for the 1820 Belfast grocer: age 24 fits, with the same trade and no continuous residence or family contradiction excluding an earlier Belfast period. This does not establish a move or identity. 3324 died in 1816 and cannot be the shopkeeper. Preserve the Rosemary Street to 34 Smith Street move without treating a shop as birthplace.

Benjamin Glasgow was a Cookstown mill partner of William Glasgow. Their 1858 action concerned interference with the River Ardtrea water supply. Benjamin had sought weir levels from John Sloan in 1856.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390574459/ Belfast News-Letter, 22 July 1858, p. 3].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390575046/ Belfast News-Letter, 23 July 1858, p. 4].</ref> He appears as Benjamin Glasgow, Esq., of Drapersfield in a December 1869 property advertisement and in a July 1870 account of land made available for the Cookstown celebration.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/388287498/ Belfast News-Letter, 22 December 1869, p. 2].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/387881589/ Belfast News-Letter, 15 July 1870, p. 4].</ref>

Benjamin Glasgow of Drapersfield, Cookstown, married Wilhelmina, eldest daughter of Richard Pike, Esq., of Beechgrove, Dungannon, at Dungannon on 16 February 1864.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/387828785/ Belfast News-Letter, 18 February 1864, p. 2].</ref>

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
Robert Glasgow and James Woods traded as Glasgow and Woods and brought an earlier mill-water action in 1842. A July 1858 report recalls that action and explicitly identifies Robert as Benjamin’s father in Benjamin’s named testimony.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390574459/ Belfast News-Letter, 22 July 1858, p.3].</ref> A January 1864 advertisement by Benjamin and William Glasgow concerns premises formerly the residence of the late Robert Glasgow; identification with the earlier partner remains to be demonstrated.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/387805714/ Belfast News-Letter, 19 January 1864, p.2].</ref>

In his named testimony, Benjamin said Robert was his father, that he managed his father’s mill from 1850 and that Robert died in 1856. Benjamin’s evidence describes a companion as “witness’s uncle, Mr. Glasgow, sen.”; identification as William belongs to the separate case context, not this quotation.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390574459/ Belfast News-Letter, 22 July 1858, p.3], Benjamin’s evidence.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
Prefer 2656: actual profile death on 20 August 1856 at Tullyveagh/Cookstown agrees with Benjamin’s directly stated 1856 father death. Retain 3941, the Coltrim householder, as a weaker rival: its structured 1831 death is an after-boundary, while its full biography says no reliable later death is established. Do not reject it for dying in 1831. Documentary Robert–Benjamin paternity is certain; profile identity and William’s brother inference stay qualified. No mother supplied.

Compare the 1864 civil marriage, 1842 court papers and mill deeds with Robert-2656 of Tullyveagh. The PRONI pre-1858 index says its original documents do not survive; do not assume a will can supply missing family details.

[[Glasgow-3941|Glasgow-3941]]: Robert of Coltrim appears in a Drapers’ Company lease in 1820, tithe in 1827 and census in 1831. The adult period fits, but Coltrim is distinct from Cookstown/Drapersfield and no mill partnership or father bridge is documented. [[Glasgow-2656|Glasgow-2656]]: Live profile checked 4 October 2026: death 20 August 1856 at Tullyveagh, Cookstown, fits the testimony’s 1856 father death and district. Its family-tree and wills-index lead require original/source review; mill identity and Margaret George’s motherhood remain unproved.

== Biography ==
Adam D. Glasgow of Broughshane appears in the Royal Belfast Academical Institution School Department prize list in June 1830, in trigonometry/astronomy, geometry and algebra.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390569859/ Belfast News-Letter, 29 June 1830, p.3, Royal Belfast Academical Institution School Department], original inspected 4 October 2026.</ref>

The Belfast College report dated 30 April 1831 names him in public mathematics examinations and, with Frederick Clarke, in the junior mathematical course and additional reading.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390545285/ Belfast News-Letter, 6 May 1831, p.3, Belfast College report dated 30 April], original inspected 4 October 2026.</ref>

A January 1837 report records his resignation as assistant in the Mathematical and Mercantile School of the Royal Belfast Institution. His class gave him Donnegan’s Greek Lexicon on 22 December 1836.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390542489/ Belfast News-Letter, 10 January 1837, p.2, resignation presentation on 22 December 1836], original inspected 4 October 2026.</ref>

Rev. Adam D. Glasgow received a unanimous call to Berry Street Presbyterian Church, Belfast, in January 1840.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390553900/ Belfast News-Letter, 17 January 1840, p.2, Berry Street ministerial call], original inspected 4 October 2026.</ref> At a soiree on 5 March 1840 the congregation presented a pulpit dress to its newly ordained minister.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390555182/ Belfast News-Letter, 10 March 1840, p.2, Berry Street soiree on 5 March], original inspected 4 October 2026.</ref>

Marriage notice: on 25 July 1840 (reported as “25th ult.”), Mr James Small, of Lottery Cottage, county Armagh, married Miss Margaret Small of this town; the officiant was Rev. Adam Glasgow. Minister/officiant occurrence, not kinship. Keep adjacent London/St George’s wedding separate. Strongly compatible with Glasgow-1781, without unique identification. <ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560450/ Belfast News-Letter, 7 August 1840, p. 3], original passage checked 5 October 2026.</ref>

Separate soirée passage: at a Tuesday-evening meeting on 27 October at the New School-house connected with the Presbyterian Church, Townsend-street, Rev. Adam Glasgow opened the proceedings; Rev. Josias Wilson closed with prayer. Do not replace/remove the existing Cookstown Academy/Robert Glasgow reading on this same page. Keep both distinct passages in one page row and one clip asset, with Adam as an additional excerpt. Strongly compatible with Glasgow-1781; no kinship. <ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390563103/ Belfast News-Letter, 30 October 1840, p. 2], original passage checked 5 October 2026.</ref>

Belfast Town Mission annual meeting in the new school-room, Fisherwick-place, was held “on Wednesday evening last”; Rev. Adam Glasgow is among listed speakers. Preserve relative date wording; do not infer 28 October. Separate anti-slavery meeting on page is unrelated. Strongly compatible with Glasgow-1781; no kinship. <ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390563260/ Belfast News-Letter, 6 November 1840, p. 2], original passage checked 5 October 2026.</ref>

General Synod report separately says ordained Ministers Messrs Adam Glasgow and James Carr offered themselves for foreign mission in India and were accepted; initial field Kathiawar/Guzerat, planned departure 4 August overland to Bombay. This is James Carr, not James Glasgow in adjacent set-apart report. Parent is coordinating separate passage with James packet; append distinct Adam target/excerpt if needed. Planned departure is not proof journey occurred. <ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/390559244/ Belfast News-Letter, 14 July 1840, p. 1], original passage checked 5 October 2026.</ref>

== Biography ==

The Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser reported two marriages at Paisley on the 25th ult: George Sherbrooke Airey, Esq., a Royal Navy lieutenant and son of the late Lieutenant-General Sir George Airey, to Anne, second daughter of the late Robert Glasgow, Esq.; and, at the same time, Rev. George Drake, son of Rev. John Drake, rector of Stourton, to Charlotte Maria Cecilia, youngest daughter of the late Robert Glasgow, Esq., of Montgreenan, Ayr. The 25 August 1847 date is inferred from ‘25th ult’ relative to the 2 September issue. The clipped passage does not include the issue header. Profile matches remain qualified; the notice names no mothers or Irish origins.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/401331272/ Freeman’s Journal and Daily Commercial Advertiser, 2 September 1847, p. 4, marriages], original passage visually checked; issue date and page verified separately.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
Prefer [[Robertson-30564]] for the late father: his actual biography describes the Robertson-to-Glasgow surname change, Montgreenan inheritance, death in 1845, and daughters Anne and Charlotte Marie Cecilia. [[Glasgow-3000]] fits Anne; [[Glasgow-3003]] fits Charlotte’s distinctive name, 1827 birth and Drake surname; [[Drake-13873]] fits Rev George. [[Glasgow-1076]] is a weaker historical alternative, whose actual biography makes the later girls descendants rather than his known daughters. These are compatible identifications; the newspaper supplies direct father/spouse statements but no mothers. George Sherbrooke Airey is the bridegroom, distinct from his father [[Airey-297]].


The printed wording is evidence for the two marriages and the stated father relationships at the level of the people named in the notice. The date 25 August 1847 is inferred from ‘25th ult’; it is not printed as a full date. The clipped passage does not show the issue header.

Candidate comparisons remain qualified. Robertson-30564 is the probable late Robert Glasgow of Montgreenan candidate: the 1847 notice calls Charlotte the youngest daughter of the late Robert Glasgow of Montgreenan; the 1827 birth notice places an unnamed daughter of Mrs Robertson Glasgow at Rome; a profile-cited 1841 census transcription lists Robert Glasgow with Charlotte, age 10, though that census has not been independently checked. The existing Montgreenan succession account connects Robertson-30564 (Robert Robertson, later using Glasgow; died 1845) with the estate. This evidence supports the candidate beyond the current tree links, but does not prove the identity. Glasgow-1076 (1747–1827) remains a weaker possible alternative because his death before 1847 is compatible with “late”; no reviewed evidence definitively excludes him. Anne Glasgow-3000 is possible; Charlotte Glasgow-3003 is strongly compatible by names, current Drake surname and 1827 birth; Rev George Drake-13873 is probable by name/title and the existing spouse link. No compatible profile for George Sherbrooke Airey was located in the bounded local search.

The previous local Open-profile summaries showed these existing tree links as unknown (tree-only), with no evidence IDs: Robertson-30564 as father of Glasgow-3000 and Glasgow-3003 (generated claims with provenance wikitree_parent_field), and Drake-13873 as spouse of Glasgow-3003 (generated claim with provenance wikitree_spouse_field). Those prior assessments describe the state of the evidence before this notice; the tree links themselves are not documentary proof. The record-level father and spouse statements are direct, but their application to the profile candidates remains pending identity confirmation. No profile relationship upgrade is claimed or applied. No mother is named or assessed.

Next checks: independently identify George Sherbrooke Airey and verify the Anne and Charlotte candidate assignments using biographical, naval, clerical, baptismal or marriage records. Reassess candidate relationship status only after identity is established.

== Biography ==
14 March 1524/25: Jhon of Glesquho is among men fined for failure to appear at the head court. On 15 March [1525/26], Jhon Glesquho is explicitly included among all the tenants of Quodquen, again for nonappearance. The latter heading omits the year; the bracketed year follows Appendix B.<ref>William Croft Dickinson (ed.), Court Book of the Barony of Carnwath 1523–1542 (1937), printed pp.31–32, 35–36 and Appendix B p.cxix; PDF 160–161; https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1271/7974/127179749.23.pdf#page=160. Printed edition inspected 15 October 2026; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

6 February 1531/32: Costin Thomsone stands surety for Jhone Glasgw’s goods. The same court names Jhone of Glasgw among Upper Quothquan tenants who forcibly recovered seized property from the barony officer after he reached Libberton. After their nonappearance and witness evidence, the court decreed forfeiture of their tenancies, holdings and movable goods on the lord’s lands, with imprisonment for a year at his will. This records a decree, not proof that imprisonment was carried out.<ref>William Croft Dickinson (ed.), Court Book of the Barony of Carnwath 1523–1542 (1937), printed pp.136–139; Appendix B p.cxxii; PDF 265–268; https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1271/7974/127179749.23.pdf#page=265. Printed edition inspected 15 October 2026; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

8 October 1532: Jhone Glasgw appears with the Upper Quothquan group in a judgment for breaking an arrestment on malt belonging to James Atzesone, held in Robert Cowan’s barn at Libberton.<ref>William Croft Dickinson (ed.), Court Book of the Barony of Carnwath 1523–1542 (1937), printed pp.142–144; Appendix B p.cxxii; PDF 271–273; https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1271/7974/127179749.23.pdf#page=271. Printed edition inspected 15 October 2026; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

The remaining indexed John passages include tenant nonappearance on May 1526 (day unresolved) and 22 January 1526/27, followed by a claim against Jhone Kello on 13 October 1530, deferred to the next court. The last record gives an adversary, not a relative. The recurring tenant names support the consolidated local identity but do not prove an inherited tenancy. The May header prints 15 May while Appendix B lists 26 May; no exact day is adopted.<ref>Dickinson (1937), printed pp.40–41,51–52,115–117; Appendix B pp.cxix,cxxi; PDF170,181,244–246; https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1271/7974/127179749.23.pdf#page=246. Printed edition inspected 15 October 2026; original manuscript uninspected.</ref>

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

The local 17 October 2026 review prefers this recorded George as the probable father of [[Glasgow-991|James Glasgow]]. His own profile identification and ancestry remain on HOLD; no second George profile is ready to create.<ref name="MuriestonFatherReview" />
George Glasgw was named in Mureistoun in the Calder barony act dated 19 April 1586, ordering a muster on 4 August. The entry establishes an obligation, not attendance.<ref>James Maidment, ed., ''Analecta Scotica'', I (1834), article CXVI, pp.395–396,399; https://archive.org/details/analectascotica00maidgoog. Printed pages inspected 15 October 2026; manuscript not inspected.</ref> McCall’s 1894 parish history repeats the same occurrence, rather than providing a second record.<ref>H.B. McCall, ''History and Antiquities of the Parish of Mid-Calder'' (1894), p.16; https://archive.org/details/historyantiquiti00mcal.</ref>

An adult George Glasgow witnessed the Mid Calder baptism on 17 February 1605 of George, son of James Glasgow, whose residence is provisionally read Muirestoun, probably Murieston. John Smith was another witness; a final witness remains unresolved. The witness’s own residence and his relationship to the father and child are not stated.<ref>National Records of Scotland, Mid Calder Old Parish Registers, 694/1, volume 10, p.7, baptism 17 February 1605; https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/; original owner-held page re-inspected 16 October 2026.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
Select George [[Glasgow-1099]] as the leading possible existing identity for the Mureistoun man of 1586, probably the 1605 adult witness. His protocol-defined 1565–1572 birth range, minority in 1586 and 1598 marriage contract are real constraints, not a 1575 birthday or proof that 1598 was his first marriage. They permit the two occurrences. The 17 October family model prefers the record-defined George as [[James-991]]'s probable father; identifying him with the merchant, and therefore [[William-3522]] upstream, remains separately uncertain. James's unsupported [[circa-1575]] estimate would conflict if proved, so no date is moved to force identity. [[Glasgow-3171]]'s age-free 1676 burial implies exceptional longevity for a 1586 adult; [[Glascoe-36]]'s reported 1589 death is unverified and would exclude the 1605 witness if confirmed. Retain both weak comparisons; no extra George son or mother is created.


=== Family reconstruction — 17 October 2026 ===

Prefer the named George of Mureistoun as [[Glasgow-991|James Glasgow]]’s probable father. George is recorded at Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder obligation; the accepted 1605 original-register reading places James’s household in probable Muirestoun and names an adult George Glasgow as witness to the baptism of James’s son George. The earlier review already assessed the two adult George occurrences as probably one man. The same uncommon surname, the probable same holding across nineteen years, and the older name-bearer’s personal participation in the younger household favour lineal family continuity. Father is the preferred degree: an older established man followed by James’s child-bearing household is a normal two-generation sequence, and the child’s George name is compatible with that reconstruction. This is a combined locality/household inference, not three independent proofs or a compulsory naming rule. The 1605 witness’s residence and age are unstated, and Muirestoun remains a probable reading/location. Shared holding names do not prove a legal title transfer. Father, uncle, older brother, cousin and neighbour remain genuine alternatives. The 1586 obligation does not establish muster attendance, and neither record states that George was James’s father. The George name and witness role are supporting context, not direct kinship. [[Glasgow-3163|Andrew Glasgow]] remains an unselected uncertain father alternative; his 1597/8 testament names Robert, Marion, Jonet and Isobel, not James. The George comparison supplies a closer holding-and-witness association than the broader Andrew/Calder model, without proving that Andrew could not be James’s father. For the working tree only, select [[Glasgow-3522|William Glasgow]] as George of Mureistoun’s uncertain father through the surviving possible identification with the Glasgow merchant [[Glasgow-1099|George Glasgow]]. Protocol 2903 explicitly names that merchant’s deceased father William; protocol 2916 gives his mother and curator. The same rare full name and compatible 1586 generation make the merchant an existing-profile comparison for the Mureistoun man. The father proof belongs to the merchant: transferring it to the Mureistoun account depends entirely on the unproved identity. This is a testable named upstream route, not direct evidence of a Calder-to-Glasgow movement or a newly proved son of William. The merchant was a minor in 1586, with the accepted approximate birth range 1565–1572. If James’s conventional circa-1575 birth were established, that would conflict with his being the merchant’s son. James’s birth is unrecorded: a later birth in the 1580s can fit the 1605 fatherhood and, toward the earlier end of George’s range, ordinary fatherhood in the previous generation. Those are compatibility examples, not new birth estimates. The 1598 marriage-contract comparison does not prove a first marriage or identify James’s mother. No date is altered to make this route fit. George-1099 stays a compatible candidate; there is no merge, no second distinct George son claimed for William, and no automatic transfer of Margaret Herbesoun or a wife as mother. If the two Georges are different men, William’s upstream placement must be reconsidered. The retained George Glascoe-36 and George-3171 comparisons remain open on their actual source limits. James’s former selected Andrew father becomes an uncertain alternative; George of Mureistoun becomes the preferred probable father. A separately uncertain William upstream link keeps the family model inspectable. The record-only George uses the existing complete sourced public subject account and is not a new WikiTree profile or an independently counted extra surname person. The 216-profile pre-1850 child side below James retains all its downstream uncertainty and possible duplicates. The working cohort’s connected components and connected pairs do not improve merely because this named intermediary is displayed. No live WikiTree save, new original inspection, mother, birth/death change or certainty upgrade is claimed.

<ref name="MuriestonFatherReview">[https://archive.org/details/analectascotica00maidgoog Maidment, Analecta Scotica I (1834), art.CXVI pp.395–396,399: Calder act 19 April1586, George Glasgw in Mureistoun; printed pages visually checked15October2026, court manuscript unread]; [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/church-registers/church-births-baptisms Mid Calder OPR694/10 p.7, 17February1605: George child of James in probable Muirestoun; adult witnesses George Glasgow and John Smith; owner-held original page reread16October2026]; [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc01scogoog/page/n113/mode/2up Renwick, Glasgow Protocols vol.9, protocol2903, printed p.103, 15July1586: George heir of deceased father William; accepted earlier reading]; [https://archive.org/details/abstractsprotoc01scogoog/page/n116/mode/2up Renwick, vol.9, protocol2916, printed p.107, 1September1586: George’s mother Margaret Herbesoun and curator Stephen; accepted earlier reading].</ref>


The 1586 man and 1605 witness are probably one person, as a working identity reviewed on 16 October 2026. The particular holding associated with the 1605 household, the local surname and a compatible 19-year adult career support that preference. The witness’s own residence is unstated; another George remains possible. The witness might be James’s father or another relative or neighbour; no parent relationship is selected. Birth date, parents, spouse, children and death are unknown. No live profile creation is recommended while compatible existing profiles are unresolved.

[[Glasgow-1099]] remains compatible with either adult occurrence but has no documented Mureistoun holding. [[Glasgow-3171]] is a very weak undated comparison requiring exceptional longevity; his 1676 burial gives no age. [[Glascoe-36]] remains compatible with the 1586 man, while the reported but unsupported 1589 death needs checking before using it to exclude the 1605 witness. [[Glasgow-1082]] is the child and cannot be either adult in this baptism.

Compare the other Mid Calder baptism pages for the same holding and witnesses, then inspect NLS MS.3724 and Beveridge’s transcript MS.3725 for George, James, heirs, leases and succession at Mureistoun. The catalogue places the 1586 land-title courts at original pp.1–15 and the chronological court sequence at pp.23–189; it records a gap between 2 May 1592 and 26 November 1594. These manuscript pages have not been read.<ref>National Library of Scotland, catalogue entries MS.3724, https://manuscripts.nls.uk/repositories/2/archival_objects/37880, and MS.3725, https://manuscripts.nls.uk/repositories/2/archival_objects/37881; catalogue consulted 15 October 2026, manuscript pages uninspected.</ref>

identity_assessment.basis: The preferred working identification is that George Glasgw in Mureistoun in the 1586 Calder muster obligation was the adult George Glasgow who witnessed the 17 February 1605 baptism of George, son of James Glasgow in provisionally read Muirestoun. The 1605 household points to the same holding as the earlier George, within the same parish setting. The surname is specific to this local comparison, and a 19-year interval is straightforward for one adult career. A child bearing George’s name and an adult George participating in his baptism make a continuing local family association more economical than two unconnected Georges. Together these observations warrant probable rather than merely possible cross-record identity. They do not amount to independent proofs of every step.
identity_assessment.limitations: The witness’s own residence is unstated, and another George in the district remains possible. The residence reading Muirestoun and its identification as Murieston remain probable. Shared spelling and locality are related observations; McCall repeats Maidment’s 1586 act and is not a second muster occurrence. Naming the child George is supporting context, not proof of a naming rule. The 1586 act records an obligation, not attendance. Neither source gives George’s age or states a relationship to James. Father, uncle, brother, other kinsman and neighbour remain alternatives. No father is changed: Andrew Glasgow-3163 remains James’s selected uncertain father, while George is an important competing paternal or collateral explanation. George Glasgow-1099, the merchant, remains compatible but unselected; the 1586 minor’s curatorship and the 1598 marriage contract do not identify him at Murieston. No mother, birth date, identity merge or confidently marked paternal edge is added.

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

Sarah Glasgow was a daughter of [[Glasgow-428|William Glasgow]] of Currituck, North Carolina. Her father named her in his will of 30 September 1746, proved 7 April 1747.<ref name="William1746">[https://www.ncgenweb.us/currituck/wills/glasgowwilliam1746.html William Glasgow will, 30 September 1746; proved 7 April 1747, North Carolina State Archives MARS 12.96.1.805; NCGenWeb published transcription checked 17 October 2026].</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Her mother, exact dates and later identity remain unknown. The will names her paternal siblings Caleb, Abiah and Elizabeth; the identification of the adult Caleb profiles remains probable. The unnamed grandfather and the wife’s unborn child are not assigned modern identities. The contingent land interest and cattle in a mark given by an unnamed grandfather belong to Sarah’s bequest; the will does not name that grandfather. The account is based on the checked published transcription; the manuscript has not been newly inspected.

No compatible modern historical profile was established in the checked scope; this draft preserves her family role without creating or merging a profile. The two Scottish baptism candidates name a different father, John.

record_matches.assessment: William Glasgow-428's 30 September 1746 will directly distinguishes daughter Sarah. Her later life is untraced; the supplied draft preserves her one family role without a mother assignment. The actual Glasgow-2451 and Glasgow-4122 accounts represent Scottish daughters of John, conflicting with Sarah's named father William. Fresh Sarah/Glasgow surname-variant searches found no compatible Glasgow/Glasco/Glascoe historical account. Fuzzy Glass/Glascock and married-surname hits are not accepted on a name score; examined nearby colonial comparisons are recorded in the duplicate audit. Do not conflate Sarah with Lowdenner, Abiah, Elizabeth or the unborn child, or infer her mother from Susanah's status as testator's wife.
